title: AI and robotics accelerate search for better gut microbiome therapies
excerpt: Biomedical engineers at Duke University have demonstrated a method for systematically developing novel, complex combinations of probiotics and prebiotics to more effectively maintain gut health and treat various gastrointestinal diseases.
content_html:
Biomedical engineers at Duke University have demonstrated a method for systematically developing novel, complex combinations of probiotics and prebiotics to more effectively maintain gut health and treat various gastrointestinal diseases.

By strategically designing experiments and robotically automating thousands of parallel trials to fill knowledge gaps and make the model more accurate, the approach can reveal complex interactions among many microbial species, nutritional sources and the surrounding environment.

One challenge in designing probiotics and prebiotics that improve gut health is the substantial variability in diet, organisms present in the gut, medications and other host factors. In a proof-of-concept study, researchers used this method to identify specific bacterial combinations and dietary fibers that together consistently promote the health and function of the human gut regardless of variability in the organisms present. The approach could be a boon for a rapidly growing prebiotic and probiotic industry that has long struggled to demonstrate consistent and predictable results for customers.

"If you take a seed and plant it in soil that is depleted of nutrients and minerals, it might not grow very well," said Ophelia Venturelli, associate professor of biomedical engineering at Duke. "The same thing applies to putting microbes into a person's gut microbiome. This work aims to engineer both the environment and the bacteria to improve human health."

The results appear online July 27 in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

A crowded and variable ecosystem

The human gut is a highly complicated environment that hosts thousands of different species of microorganisms. The number of microbial cells in the human gut is roughly equal to the number of human cells, and they weigh up to nearly half a pound (225 grams).

To further complicate matters, the makeup of species and their relative ratios vary greatly from region to region and even from person to person, depending on a wide range of factors like diet, lifestyle and environmental exposures. Although bacterial groups in the human gut microbiome have much in common, different people harbor different bacterial species, creating substantial variability that can make treating disruptions in their functions difficult.

And disruptions can be serious. Microbes in the gut prevent unwanted pathogens from taking hold while breaking down food like dietary fiber and complex carbohydrates that the stomach can't. This process provides nutrients essential for the health of gastrointestinal cells. Bacteria also produce other molecules that shape immune system development, energy balance, cardiometabolic health and even brain and neurological activities.

Searching trillions of combinations

To address these issues, introducing healthy microbial communities and making sure they have the nutrients they need to thrive has become a major industry, currently valued at about $130 billion worldwide. Demonstrating consistent results, however, has remained a challenge.

"Probiotics alone might not be able to colonize a person's gut long enough to do anything helpful because there's so much living there already," Venturelli said. "There is substantial uncertainty about whether these current methods for restoring gut microbiome health are effective at all, since outcomes are still largely unpredictable."

Venturelli's new approach is meant to bring more predictability to the whole enterprise.

In the new paper, Venturelli and her colleagues demonstrate a method for intelligently and systematically exploring this large design space by closing the loop between experiments and computational models. In benchtop experiments, her team forced various combinations of 15 different species of gut microbes to live and eat together. Their menu consisted of six types of dietary fibers known to affect the production of butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid critical to gut health.

Even with just 21 different variables on the table, the potential combinations of microbes and their diets easily numbered well into the trillions. Faced with such an intractable problem, the researchers turned to machine learning, computer models, automated experiments and active learning—also known as Bayesian optimization.

Bayesian optimization is an approach that designs experiments to simultaneously fill gaps in the computer model and achieve specific goals. Armed with autonomous robotic experimental systems, the team was able to plow through five batches of high-throughput experiments—up to 390 conditions at the same time—to build their knowledge of interactions and outcomes.

"We found a lot of unexpected effects from interactions between the microbes and the fibers," Venturelli said. "These effects are very complicated and couldn't have been predicted before we ran the experiments."

A butyrate-producing trio emerges

The results revealed that the dietary fiber inulin, along with two inulin-hungry microbial species (Bacteroides uniformis and Anaerostipes caccae), interacted with a third bacterial species (Prevotella copri) to reliably produce the desired butyrate. What's more, this combination remained effective regardless of what other species and factors were introduced.

The researchers are now working to see whether this combination can effectively treat a mouse model of inflammatory bowel disease, with promising early results. Beyond this specific combination, the researchers believe their approach could be used to discover many more promising combinations for a wide range of gastrointestinal disorders.

"There are companies combining bacteria and dietary fibers in their gut health products already, but they are not yet trying to identify and match the right synergies to the right problem," Venturelli said. "I believe using this process would help create more tailored—and more effective—solutions to a wide range of gastrointestinal issues."

Publication details

content_html_zh:
杜克大学的生物医学工程师展示了一种系统开发益生菌和益生元的新颖、复杂组合的方法，以更有效地维持肠道健康并治疗各种胃肠道疾病。

通过战略性地设计实验并自动执行数千个平行试验来填补知识空白并使模型更加准确，该方法可以揭示许多微生物物种、营养来源和周围环境之间复杂的相互作用。

设计改善肠道健康的益生菌和益生元面临的一大挑战是饮食、肠道中存在的生物体、药物和其他宿主因素的巨大变化。 在一项概念验证研究中，研究人员使用这种方法来识别特定的细菌组合和膳食纤维，无论存在的生物体如何变化，这些组合和膳食纤维都能够持续促进人类肠道的健康和功能。 对于快速发展的益生元和益生菌行业来说，这种方法可能是一个福音，该行业长期以来一直在努力向客户展示一致和可预测的结果。

杜克大学生物医学工程副教授奥菲莉亚·文图雷利 (Ophelia Venturelli) 表示：“如果你将一颗种子种植在缺乏营养和矿物质的土壤中，它可能不会生长得很好。” “同样的情况也适用于将微生物放入人的肠道微生物组中。 这项工作旨在对环境和细菌进行改造，以改善人类健康。”

研究结果于 7 月 27 日在线发表在《自然化学生物学》杂志上。

拥挤且多变的生态系统

人类肠道是一个高度复杂的环境，栖息着数千种不同种类的微生物。 人体肠道中微生物细胞的数量大致等于人体细胞的数量，重量可达近半磅（225克）。

更复杂的是，物种的构成及其相对比例因地区、甚至因人而异，这取决于饮食、生活方式和环境暴露等多种因素。 尽管人类肠道微生物组中的细菌群有很多共同点，但不同的人拥有不同的细菌种类，从而产生巨大的变异性，使得治疗其功能中断变得困难。

中断可能会很严重。 肠道中的微生物可以防止有害病原体的侵入，同时分解胃无法分解的食物，例如膳食纤维和复合碳水化合物。 这个过程提供了胃肠细胞健康所必需的营养物质。 细菌还产生其他影响免疫系统发育、能量平衡、心脏代谢健康甚至大脑和神经活动的分子。

搜索数万亿种组合

为了解决这些问题，引入健康的微生物群落并确保它们拥有茁壮成长所需的营养已成为一个主要产业，目前全球价值约 1300 亿美元。 然而，展示一致的结果仍然是一个挑战。

Venturelli 说：“仅靠益生菌可能无法在人的肠道内定植足够长的时间，从而发挥任何作用，因为那里已经有太多益生菌了。” “目前这些恢复肠道微生物健康的方法是否有效，存在很大的不确定性，因为结果在很大程度上仍然是不可预测的。”

Venturelli 的新方法旨在为整个企业带来更多的可预测性。

在这篇新论文中，Venturelli 和她的同事展示了一种通过关闭实验和计算模型之间的循环来智能、系统地探索这个巨大设计空间的方法。 在台式实验中，她的团队迫使 15 种不同肠道微生物的各种组合一起生活和进食。 他们的菜单包含六种已知会影响丁酸盐产生的膳食纤维，丁酸盐是一种对肠道健康至关重要的短链脂肪酸。

即使只有 21 个不同的变量，微生物及其饮食的潜在组合也很容易达到数万亿个。 面对如此棘手的问题，研究人员转向机器学习、计算机模型、自动化实验和主动学习（也称为贝叶斯优化）。

贝叶斯优化是一种设计实验以同时填补计算机模型中的空白并实现特定目标的方法。 借助自主机器人实验系统，该团队能够进行五批高通量实验（同时进行多达 390 个条件），以建立关于相互作用和结果的知识。

“我们发现微生物和纤维之间的相互作用产生了许多意想不到的效果，”文图雷利说。 “这些影响非常复杂，在我们进行实验之前无法预测。”

产生丁酸盐的三重奏出现

结果显示，膳食纤维菊粉以及两种需要菊粉的微生物物种（统一拟杆菌和Anaerostipes caccae）与第三种细菌物种（普氏菌）相互作用，可靠地产生所需的丁酸盐。 更重要的是，无论引入什么其他物种和因素，这种组合仍然有效。

研究人员现在正在研究这种组合是否可以有效治疗炎症性肠病小鼠模型，并取得有希望的早期结果。 除了这种特定的组合之外，研究人员相信他们的方法还可以用于发现许多更有希望的组合来治疗各种胃肠道疾病。

Venturelli 说：“已经有一些公司将细菌和膳食纤维结合到他们的肠道健康产品中，但他们还没有尝试确定正确的协同作用并将其与正确的问题相匹配。” “我相信使用这个过程将有助于为各种胃肠道问题创造更量身定制且更有效的解决方案。”
